claim: A tradeoff exists between stereotypy and flexibility in animal locomotion, where fast long-distance travelling requires coherent regular motions, while local sampling and area-restricted search rely on flexible movements.
source: In animal locomotion a tradeoff exists between stereotypy and flexibility: fast long-distance travelling (LDT) requires coherent regular motions, while local sampling and area-restricted search (ARS) rely on flexible movements.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract without specific experimental data provided in this sentence, drawing on established knowledge about animal locomotion strategies.

claim: C. elegans locomotion can be explained as a composite of two modes: regular undulations versus flexible turning.
source: Using quantitative posture analysis we explain worm locomotion as a composite of two modes: regular undulations versus flexible turning.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative posture analysis presented in the manuscript, particularly the eigenworm decomposition shown in Figure 2.

claim: Graded reciprocal regulation of undulation and turning modes allows animals to flexibly adapt their locomotion strategy under sensory stimulation along a spectrum ranging from LDT to ARS.
source: Graded reciprocal regulation of both modes allows animals to flexibly adapt their locomotion strategy under sensory stimulation along a spectrum ranging from LDT to ARS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing gradual changes in undulation and turning amplitudes in response to oxygen stimuli, as shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: The interneurons AVK and DVA utilize FLP-1 and NLP-12 neuropeptides to control both motor modes.
source: Using genetics and functional imaging of neural activity we characterize the counteracting interneurons AVK and DVA that utilize FLP-1 and NLP-12 neuropeptides to control both motor modes.
evidence: This is supported by genetic manipulation experiments and calcium imaging data presented in Figures 5-8.

claim: Gradual regulation of behaviors via the AVK/FLP-1 and DVA/NLP-12 system is required for spatial navigation during chemotaxis.
source: Gradual regulation of behaviors via this system is required for spatial navigation during chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assay data showing defects in navigation in mutant animals, as presented in Figures 9-10.

claim: Under the assumption that food is nearby, a large variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species including mammals perform local or area-restricted search (ARS) consisting of short moves and frequent high-angled turns.
source: Under the assumption that food is nearby, a large variety of invertebrate and vertebrate species including mammals perform local or area-restricted search (ARS) consisting of short moves and frequent high-angled turns.
evidence: This statement references general knowledge about animal foraging behavior across species, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: In order to localize more distant food sources, animals disperse via long-distance travelling (LDT) by moving along straight paths.
source: Alternatively, in order to localize more distant food sources, animals disperse via long-distance travelling (LDT) by moving along straight paths (Bell, 1990; Fryxell et al., 2008; Hills, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on animal foraging strategies.

claim: C. elegans advances via undulatory crawling movements.
source: Nematodes advance via undulatory crawling movements (Gray, 1953), which can be precisely quantified (Brown et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2008; Yemini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing C. elegans locomotion.

claim: The animal's posture is tightly coupled to ventral and dorsal body wall muscle activity and therefore a reliable proxy to characterize the motor patterns underlying gait production.
source: The animal's posture is tightly coupled to ventral and dorsal body wall muscle activity and therefore a reliable proxy to characterize the motor patterns underlying gait production (Butler et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work establishing the relationship between posture and muscle activity.

claim: When removed from food C. elegans performs frequent reorientation maneuvers, which consist of brief periods of backward crawling (reversals) followed by sharp turning (omega turns).
source: When removed from food C. elegans performs frequent reorientation maneuvers, which consist of brief periods of backward crawling (reversals) followed by sharp turning (omega turns); however, when no food is detected for a prolonged time C. elegans maintains forward crawling and only infrequently reorients.
evidence: This describes known behavioral patterns of C. elegans in response to food removal, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: When no food is detected for a prolonged time C. elegans maintains forward crawling and only infrequently reorients.
source: When removed from food C. elegans performs frequent reorientation maneuvers, which consist of brief periods of backward crawling (reversals) followed by sharp turning (omega turns); however, when no food is detected for a prolonged time C. elegans maintains forward crawling and only infrequently reorients.
evidence: This describes known behavioral patterns of C. elegans in response to prolonged food absence, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: These two locomotion strategies have been explicitly characterized as ARS after removal from food and LDT.
source: These two locomotion strategies have been explicitly characterized as ARS after removal from food and LDT (Calhoun et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Peliti et al., 2013; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature characterizing these behavioral strategies.

claim: Two major locomotion strategies for goal-directed chemotaxis have been observed: the biased random walk and weathervaning.
source: Also, two major locomotion strategies for goal-directed chemotaxis have been observed: the biased random walk, which is reminiscent of bacterial chemotaxis (Berg and Brown, 1972), where animals modulate the probability of reorientation depending on sensory history (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and weathervaning, where animals directly steer toward the favored direction by introducing a subtle bias to their path (Iino and Yoshida, 2009 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing chemotaxis strategies in C. elegans.

claim: In the biased random walk strategy, animals modulate the probability of reorientation depending on sensory history.
source: Also, two major locomotion strategies for goal-directed chemotaxis have been observed: the biased random walk, which is reminiscent of bacterial chemotaxis (Berg and Brown, 1972), where animals modulate the probability of reorientation depending on sensory history (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and weathervaning, where animals directly steer toward the favored direction by introducing a subtle bias to their path (Iino and Yoshida, 2009 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work describing the biased random walk strategy.

claim: In weathervaning, animals directly steer toward the favored direction by introducing a subtle bias to their path.
source: Also, two major locomotion strategies for goal-directed chemotaxis have been observed: the biased random walk, which is reminiscent of bacterial chemotaxis (Berg and Brown, 1972), where animals modulate the probability of reorientation depending on sensory history (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999), and weathervaning, where animals directly steer toward the favored direction by introducing a subtle bias to their path (Iino and Yoshida, 2009 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work describing the weathervaning strategy.

claim: In nature, C. elegans is found in association with anthropogenic soil habitats constituting complex environments rich in olfactory cues.
source: In nature, C. elegans is found in association with anthropogenic soil habitats constituting complex environments rich in olfactory cues (Félix and Braendle, 2010; Félix and Duveau, 2012), in which local O2 concentrations vary and might serve to indicate the presence of bacterial food, pathogens or predators (Sexstone et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing C. elegans natural habitats.

claim: Local O2 concentrations in C. elegans natural habitats vary and might serve to indicate the presence of bacterial food, pathogens or predators.
source: In nature, C. elegans is found in association with anthropogenic soil habitats constituting complex environments rich in olfactory cues (Félix and Braendle, 2010; Félix and Duveau, 2012), in which local O2 concentrations vary and might serve to indicate the presence of bacterial food, pathogens or predators (Sexstone et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents speculation about the ecological significance of oxygen variation.

claim: In the laboratory, worms are fed on E. coli lawns, which generate steep O2 gradients ranging from atmospheric 21% down to 12% O2.
source: In the laboratory, worms are fed on E. coli lawns, which generate steep O2 gradients ranging from atmospheric 21% down to 12% O2 (Gray et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing oxygen gradients in laboratory conditions.

claim: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons.
source: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons (Zimmer et al., 2009), and during navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations (Cheung et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2004; Zimmer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing BAG neuron responses.

claim: During navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations.
source: A sudden decline in O2 levels activates BAG class O2 sensory neurons (Zimmer et al., 2009), and during navigation of spatial O2 gradients, animals accumulate at intermediate concentrations (Cheung et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2004; Zimmer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing O2 chemotaxis behavior.

claim: Interneuron circuits that are involved in locomotory responses to changes in ambient O2 and that communicate with O2 sensory neurons have been partially described.
source: Interneuron circuits that are involved in locomotory responses to changes in ambient O2 and that communicate with O2 sensory neurons have been partially described (Busch et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2015; Laurent et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing interneuron circuits involved in oxygen responses.

claim: The navigational strategies used during O2 chemotaxis are uncharacterized.
source: However, the navigational strategies used during O2 chemotaxis are uncharacterized.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: An immediate drop from atmospheric 21% to 10% O2 evoked a variety of behavioral changes, including transient reduction of locomotion speed and concomitant up-regulation of reversals and omega turns.
source: An immediate drop from atmospheric 21% to 10% O2 (O2 downshift) evoked a variety of behavioral changes, including transient reduction of locomotion speed and concomitant up-regulation of reversals and omega turns as previously described (Zimmer et al., 2009) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and is consistent with previously published results.

claim: O2 downshift caused up-regulation of shallow turning maneuvers during forward movement, evident as increased curvature of the animals' locomotion trajectories.
source: In addition, we observed up-regulation of shallow turning maneuvers during forward movement, evident as increased curvature of the animals' locomotion trajectories (track curvature) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The compound effect of behavioral changes upon O2 downshift was a drastic reduction in the spatial displacement of worms during the first three minutes.
source: The compound effect of these behavioral changes was a drastic reduction in the spatial displacement of worms during the first three minutes upon O2 downshift (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A sudden drop in environmental O2 concentrations evoked a change in the locomotion strategy switching from predominantly forward crawling to a mixture of reduced crawling and increased reorientations, i.e. from LDT to O2-induced ARS.
source: Thus, a sudden drop in environmental O2 concentrations evoked a change in the locomotion strategy switching from predominantly forward crawling to a mixture of reduced crawling and increased reorientations, i.e. from LDT to O2-induced ARS (see also Video 1 and Video 2 upper left panel).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Videos 1-2.

claim: This interpretation is in accordance with previous literature classifying similar behavioral strategy changes in the context of removal from food.
source: This interpretation is in accordance with previous literature classifying similar behavioral strategy changes in the context of removal from food (Calhoun et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Hills et al., 2004; Peliti et al., 2013; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing similar behavioral changes.

claim: The changes in behavioral parameters all depended on an O2 chemosensory neuron pair, termed BAG.
source: The changes in behavioral parameters all depended on an O2 chemosensory neuron pair, termed BAG, which is activated upon O2 downshift (Zimmer et al., 2009) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon O2 downshift, animals tended to stop forward locomotion and adopted complex and variable postures, unlike the more regular sinusoid-like postures associated with LDT.
source: Upon O2 downshift, animals tended to stop forward locomotion and adopted complex and variable postures, unlike the more regular sinusoid-like postures associated with LDT (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by visual observations shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: LDT was associated with long stretches of regular and coherent body posture patterns, while O2-induced ARS after O2 downshift exhibited variability in the amplitude, direction and frequency of body postural changes.
source: LDT was associated with long stretches of regular and coherent body posture patterns, while O2-induced ARS after O2 downshift exhibited variability in the amplitude, direction and frequency of body postural changes (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by posture kymograph data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Shallow turns, slowing bouts, reversals and omega turns occurred sparsely during LDT; however, during O2-induced ARS these behaviors were up-regulated 2-4-fold.
source: Note that shallow turns, slowing bouts, reversals and omega turns also occurred sparsely during LDT; however, during O2-induced ARS these behaviors were up-regulated 2-4-fold (compare pre- with post- stimulus period in all panels of Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparisons of behavioral parameters shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Principal components analysis (PCA) calculates the eigenvectors (termed eigenworms, EWs) of the covariance matrix of inter-segment angles observed over many posture time series.
source: Briefly, in this approach, principal components analysis (PCA) (Jolliffe, 2002) calculates the eigenvectors (termed eigenworms, EWs) of the covariance matrix of inter-segment angles observed over many posture time series (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the mathematical method used, with a citation to the PCA methodology and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Linear combinations of the first four EWs account for the gross majority (>85%) of the observed postural variance.
source: EW's are a set of representative worm postures (as defined by a vector of inter-segment angles), in descending order of explanatory power; i.e. each EW contributes a certain amount of postural variance and linear combinations of the first four EWs account for the gross majority (>85%) of the observed postural variance (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Despite the strong effect of O2 downshift on the animals' postures, the respective underlying EWs were nearly identical.
source: We found that despite the strong effect of O2 downshift on the animals' postures, the respective underlying EWs were nearly identical (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of eigenworms calculated from pre- and post-stimulus data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The percentage of total variance explained by EW1 and EW2 decreased whereas the percentage of total variance explained by lower-order EWs increased after O2 downshift.
source: However, the relative contributions of each EW changed: the percentage of total variance explained by EW1 and EW2 decreased whereas the percentage of total variance explained by lower-order EWs increased (e.g. EW3-6, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The different postures observed during LDT versus O2-induced ARS can be described by linear combinations of the same elementary shapes, the relative weights of which are modulated upon stimulation.
source: Thus, the different postures observed during LDT versus O2-induced ARS can be described by linear combinations of the same elementary shapes, the relative weights of which are modulated upon stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eigenworm analysis data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The combination of EW1 and 2 corresponds to the regular undulatory movements along the worm's body, which generates forward and backward crawling.
source: The combination of EW1 and 2 corresponds to the regular undulatory movements along the worm's body, which generates forward and backward crawling (Stephens et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing the meaning of the first two eigenworms.

claim: Strong transients in the residual time series (turning mode) coincided with shallow turns as well as with highly bent omega turns.
source: Subtracting the undulation mode from the full body posture time series, which is equivalent to reconstructing posture time series based on all remaining EWs 3–24, revealed a strikingly organized residual mode. Strong transients in the residual time series coincided with shallow turns as well as with highly bent omega turns (see Figure 2C for examples); we thus termed this time series the 'turning mode'.
evidence: This is supported by visual analysis of posture kymographs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The turning mode was qualitatively different in comparison to the undulation mode: the head moved in anti-phase with the tail and in phase with the mid-body whereas the undulation mode was generated by anti-phase undulations of head and mid-body and in phase undulation of head and tail.
source: The turning mode was qualitatively different in comparison to the undulation mode: the head moved in anti-phase with the tail and in phase with the mid-body whereas the undulation mode was generated by anti-phase undulations of head and mid-body and in phase undulation of head and tail.
evidence: This describes the qualitative characteristics of the two modes based on analysis of body segment movements.

claim: The undulation mode and turning mode were not independent as they were often phase-locked: signal cross-correlation analysis showed that the onset of turning movements lagged on average ~0.6 s behind the undulation mode.
source: The undulation mode and turning mode were not independent as they were often phase-locked: signal cross-correlation analysis showed that the onset of turning movements lagged on average ~0.6 s behind the undulation mode (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The diverse and complex postures observed in worms were obtained by simple linear addition of undulation and turning shapes.
source: The diverse and complex postures observed in worms were obtained by simple linear addition of undulation and turning shapes (Figure 2D; Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reconstructed worm shapes shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claim: Apparently complex postures of C. elegans can be linearly composed out of simpler elementary shapes, which constitute behaviorally relevant motor patterns of the worm: the undulation mode describes regular forward and backward crawling, onto which the turning mode imposes turning movements.
source: In conclusion, apparently complex postures of C. elegans can be linearly composed out of simpler elementary shapes, which constitute behaviorally relevant motor patterns of the worm: the undulation mode describes regular forward and backward crawling, onto which the turning mode imposes turning movements.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the eigenworm decomposition analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Biomechanical calculations indicate that both body bending amplitude and frequency synergistically generate thrust against the substrate thereby contributing to the animals' locomotion speed.
source: Biomechanical calculations indicate that both body bending amplitude and frequency synergistically generate thrust against the substrate thereby contributing to the animals' locomotion speed (Gray, 1953).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous biomechanical work.

claim: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction.
source: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction (see Figure 3A for examples); track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 3A and quantitative analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: Track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude.
source: High signals in turning amplitude consistently coincided with regions of high track curvature, i.e. events when animals adjusted their heading direction (see Figure 3A for examples); track curvature was a graded function of turning amplitude (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Turning amplitude and undulation amplitude exhibited a graded inverse relationship to each other.
source: Turning amplitude and undulation amplitude exhibited a graded inverse relationship to each other (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Undulation frequency exhibited a tight linear relationship with translational locomotion speed.
source: As expected, undulation frequency exhibited a tight linear relationship with translational locomotion speed (Figure 3D) (See also reference [Stephens et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D and is consistent with previous work.

claim: Directional changes during forward movement were associated with slow locomotion: there was an inverse relationship between undulation frequency and centroid track curvature.
source: We found that directional changes during forward movement were associated with slow locomotion: there was an inverse relationship between undulation frequency and centroid track curvature (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: High undulation amplitude was associated with fast locomotion (high undulation frequency) whereas high turning amplitude was associated with slow, low-frequency locomotion.
source: High undulation amplitude was associated with fast locomotion (high undulation frequency) whereas high turning amplitude was associated with slow, low-frequency locomotion (Figures 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: All relationships between turning amplitude, undulation amplitude, undulation frequency, speed, and track curvature were preserved during both pre- and post-stimulus periods.
source: All relationships described were preserved during both pre- and post- stimulus periods (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from pre- and post-stimulus periods shown in Figure 3B-F.

claim: During turning maneuvers, animals reduce the amplitude and speed of undulation motions, leading to slow locomotion.
source: In conclusion, turning amplitude, undulation amplitude and undulation frequency are coupled: during turning maneuvers, animals reduce the amplitude and speed of undulation motions, leading to slow locomotion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the quantitative relationships shown in Figure 3.

claim: During periods of fast locomotion turning maneuvers are suppressed.
source: Contrarily during periods of fast locomotion turning maneuvers are suppressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverse relationship between turning amplitude and locomotion speed shown in Figure 3.

claim: Under the experimental conditions used, the coupling of motor parameters is a robust property of worm locomotion during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked behaviors.
source: Under our experimental conditions, the coupling of these motor parameters is a robust property of worm locomotion during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that relationships between motor parameters are preserved across different behavioral contexts.

claim: Upon stimulus onset, the mean amplitudes of turning and undulation modes were abruptly up- or down-regulated, respectively, and gradually returned to baseline within three minutes.
source: Upon stimulus onset, the mean amplitudes were abruptly up- or down-regulated, respectively, and gradually returned to baseline within three minutes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Total body amplitude changed upon stimulation with a biphasic response profile, i.e. initial suppression followed by transient up-regulation.
source: For comparison, we calculated the time course of total body amplitude, which changed upon stimulation with a biphasic response profile, i.e. initial suppression followed by transient up-regulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A gradual O2 ramp from 21% to 4% O2 caused a subtle change in mean total body amplitude but stronger and gradual reciprocal changes in mean undulation and turning amplitudes.
source: To test this hypothesis, we stimulated the animals with a temporal oxygen ramp ranging from atmospheric 21% to 4% O2 (-0.01%/s). This protocol caused a subtle change in mean total body amplitude but stronger and gradual reciprocal changes in mean undulation and turning amplitudes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The skew of turning amplitude distribution functions gradually increased towards higher levels during the oxygen ramp, without showing bimodality.
source: We then plotted the fraction of postures with a given turning amplitude as distribution functions during subsequent time segments of the ramp. We did not observe bimodality but instead that the skew of these distributions gradually increased towards higher levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by distribution analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Animals were able to gradually adjust turning and undulation motions within a wide continuous range.
source: Thus, animals were able to gradually adjust turning and undulation motions within a wide continuous range, as further revealed in a two-dimensional density plot of turning amplitude against undulation frequency (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by 2D density plot analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Oxygen stimulation results in a shift in the contributions of undulation and turning motor patterns.
source: In summary, oxygen stimulation results in a shift in the contributions of undulation and turning motor patterns.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Animals display control of the strength of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and gradually changing environments.
source: Animals display control of the strength of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and gradually changing environments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: LDT and O2-induced ARS behaviors appear to lie on a continuum of behavioral mode compositions.
source: LDT and O2-induced ARS behaviors appear to lie on a continuum of behavioral mode compositions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gradual nature of behavioral changes observed in response to oxygen stimuli.

claim: flp-1 mutants have been reported to exhibit elevated body curvature and locomotion speed.
source: flp-1 mutants have been reported to exhibit elevated body curvature and locomotion speed (Chang et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing flp-1 mutant phenotypes.

claim: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA.
source: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA; interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Garrison et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing NLP-12 expression and function.

claim: Interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed.
source: NLP-12 neuropeptides have been reported to be exclusively released from the proprioceptive interneuron DVA; interfering with the DVA/NLP-12 system leads to decreased body curvature and locomotion speed (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Garrison et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2011; Janssen et al., 2008; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing DVA/NLP-12 function.

claim: All previously reported phenotypes of flp-1 and nlp-12 mutants, DVA ablated animals, and transgenic nlp-12 rescue strains could be recapitulated in 1 hr fasted worms.
source: We assayed flp-1 and nlp-12 mutants, DVA ablated (DVA-) animals, as well as transgenic nlp-12 rescue strains in DVA, and found that all phenotypes could be recapitulated in 1 hr fasted worms (Figure 5A,B; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A,B and 6A.

claim: flp-1 expression in the single ventral ganglion interneuron class AVK is sufficient to restore a wild type phenotype.
source: We found that flp-1 expression in the single ventral ganglion interneuron class AVK, which we observed to be the neuron class with strongest expression, is sufficient to restore a wild type phenotype (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: AVK ablation caused enhanced body posture amplitude similar to flp-1 mutants.
source: We generated AVK- animals, which caused enhanced body posture amplitude similar to flp-1 mutants (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants as well as AVK-;DVA- animals exhibited intermediate total body amplitude similar to wild type levels, indicating an antagonism between both systems.
source: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants as well as AVK-;DVA- animals exhibited intermediate total body amplitude similar to wild type levels, indicating an antagonism between both systems (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B and represents an inference about the relationship between the two systems.

claim: Interfering with AVK/FLP-1 function increased undulation amplitude, while interfering with DVA/NLP-12 decreased undulation amplitude.
source: The decomposition revealed that a large proportion of altered body posture across all phenotypes could be explained by a corresponding effect on undulation amplitude. Interfering with AVK/FLP-1 function increased undulation amplitude, while interfering with DVA/NLP-12 decreased undulation amplitude . flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants exhibited intermediate phenotypes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by eigenworm decomposition analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All genotypes except flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants and DVA- animals showed an increase in turning amplitude, which was especially strong for flp-1 mutants and animals lacking AVK.
source: In addition, all genotypes except flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants and DVA- animals showed an increase in turning amplitude, which was especially strong for flp-1 mutants and animals lacking AVK (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: To a large extent the postures of mutants and manipulated strains reflected postures that were exhibited, however less frequently, by wild type animals.
source: A comparison of 2D probability density distributions of undulation vs. turning mode revealed that to a large extent the postures of mutants and manipulated strains reflected postures that were exhibited, however less frequently, by wild type animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D density distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: All analyzed mutant and cell ablation strains were compromised in regulating undulation and turning mode in response to O2 downshift.
source: Besides their effects on worm postures at constant atmospheric O2 levels, all analyzed mutant and cell ablation strains were compromised in regulating undulation and turning mode in response to O2 downshift.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the stimulus-evoked behavioral defects observed across multiple genotypes.

claim: The strongest defects in stimulus-evoked postural changes were seen in strains lacking AVK neurons, as well as in flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants.
source: The strongest defects in stimulus-evoked postural changes were seen in strains lacking AVK neurons, as well as in flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of stimulus-evoked changes shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems were both implicated in controlling locomotion speed.
source: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems were both implicated in controlling locomotion speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion speed analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK partially restored the respective phenotypes.
source: Cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK partially restored the respective phenotypes, confirming these cells as important release sites for the respective neuropeptides (Figure 6A–F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6A-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,E.

claim: In the O2 ramp paradigm, flp-1;nlp-12 double mutant animals' modulation of undulation and turning amplitudes was largely compromised.
source: However, we hypothesized that if the neuropeptides were part of a control system of worm postures, the double mutants should lack control over the composition of behavioral modes. Indeed, in the ramp paradigm the mutant animals' modulation of undulation and turning amplitudes was largely compromised (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by oxygen ramp experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phenotype of flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants in the ramp paradigm could be rescued by cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK.
source: This phenotype could be rescued by cell-specific expression of nlp-12 in DVA and flp-1 in AVK (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Control of the composition of undulation and turning modes can be partially dissected at the genetic and single neuron level.
source: In conclusion, control of the composition of undulation and turning modes can be partially dissected at the genetic and single neuron level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the genetic and cellular manipulation experiments presented in Figures 5-6.

claim: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems are required for normal body posture during LDT in constant environmental conditions as well as for the differential fine control of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and smoothly changing environments.
source: The DVA/NLP-12 and AVK/FLP-1 systems are required for normal body posture during LDT in constant environmental conditions as well as for the differential fine control of undulation and turning motions in response to both abruptly and smoothly changing environments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the genetic and cellular manipulation experiments presented in Figures 5-6.

claim: Decomposition of posture into undulation and turning modes is not only a useful quantitative description of behavior, but these motor patterns are under differential neural control.
source: Our data suggest that decomposition of posture into undulation and turning modes is not only a useful quantitative description of behavior, but that these motor patterns are under differential neural control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that genetic manipulations differentially affect the two motor modes.

claim: AVK Ca2+ signals in average decreased upon O2 downshift in freely moving animals.
source: We observed frequent Ca2+ transients of varying magnitude, which were associated with changes in the animal's locomotion speed. Consistent with this observation, AVK Ca2+ signals in average decreased upon O2 downshift (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: AVK activity did not show O2 downshift-evoked changes in immobilized animals.
source: When measuring AVK activity in immobilized animals, we did not detect O2 downshift-evoked activity changes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data from immobilized animals shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In freely moving animals, AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed.
source: In freely moving animals, we found that AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed (Figure 7D), but unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed (Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014), AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: Unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed, AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement.
source: In freely moving animals, we found that AVK activity positively correlated with locomotion speed (Figure 7D), but unlike previously reported speed-encoding interneurons, which exclusively encode either forward or reverse locomotion speed (Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014), AVK correlated with speed during both forward and reverse movement (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E and comparison with previous literature.

claim: AVK activity negatively correlated with turning amplitude during forward movement.
source: Consistent with our findings that speed and turning motions were reciprocally regulated, AVK activity negatively correlated with turning amplitude during forward movement (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The relationship of AVK activity with behavioral output was unchanged when comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods.
source: The relationship of AVK activity with behavioral output was unchanged when comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis comparing pre- and post-stimulus periods shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: Elevated AVK neuronal activity reflects high locomotion speed and low turning amplitude, thus corresponding to aspects of motion rather than to sensory inputs.
source: In summary, elevated AVK neuronal activity reflects high locomotion speed and low turning amplitude, thus corresponding to aspects of motion rather than to sensory inputs; similar observations have been made for many interneurons in C. elegans (Kato et al., 2015; Larsch et al., 2013; Laurent et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the AVK calcium imaging data, with citations to similar findings in other interneurons.

claim: The neural activity of AVK is consistent with the behavioral phenotypes of AVK- animals, which exhibit reduced locomotion speed and strong up-regulation of turning maneuvers.
source: The neural activity is consistent with the behavioral phenotypes of AVK- animals, which exhibit reduced locomotion speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and strong up-regulation of turning maneuvers (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the neural activity data with the behavioral phenotype data.

claim: AVK activity promotes locomotion speed and suppresses turning.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that AVK activity promotes locomotion speed and suppresses turning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between AVK activity and behavioral parameters.

claim: AVK can influence locomotion speed and turning suppression only in the context of feedback from the motor system.
source: However, since AVK activity changes are low in immobilized worms we propose that AVK can influence these functions only in the context of feedback from the motor system.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that AVK activity changes are reduced in immobilized animals.

claim: DVA Ca2+ signals increased on average upon O2 downshift in freely moving animals.
source: DVA Ca2+ signals increased on average upon O2 downshift (Figure 8B,C upper panel, see Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B for motion artifact controls).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: DVA activity rose on average at the transition from forward to backward directed movement.
source: We found that DVA activity correlated with multiple aspects of locomotory behavior: DVA activity rose on average at the transition from forward to backward directed movement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) and DVA was strongly activated during periods of paused locomotion (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, G), a behavior that was observed more frequently upon O2 downshift (Figure 8—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: DVA was strongly activated during periods of paused locomotion.
source: We found that DVA activity correlated with multiple aspects of locomotory behavior: DVA activity rose on average at the transition from forward to backward directed movement (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) and DVA was strongly activated during periods of paused locomotion (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, G), a behavior that was observed more frequently upon O2 downshift (Figure 8—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: After restricting the analysis exclusively to periods of forward locomotion, no O2 downshift-evoked change in the residual DVA activity was detected.
source: After restricting the analysis exclusively to periods of forward locomotion, i.e. removing reversal and pausing periods from the data, we did not detect any O2 downshift-evoked change in the residual DVA activity (Figure 8C, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data analysis shown in Figure 8C lower panel.

claim: A global correlation analysis did not detect a relationship between DVA activity and forward locomotion speed, turning amplitude or undulation amplitude.
source: In contrast to AVK, a global correlation analysis did not detect a relationship between DVA activity and forward locomotion speed, turning amplitude or undulation amplitude (R = -0.04, R = 0.09, R = 0.06, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of DVA activity with behavioral parameters.

claim: DVA Ca2+ signals were on average associated with transient increases in undulation amplitude and transient decreases in turning amplitude.
source: To test whether these signals had a behavioral correlate, we calculated Ca2+ peak-triggered averages of undulation amplitude, turning amplitude and body posture amplitude. This approach showed that DVA Ca2+ signals were on average associated with transient increases in undulation amplitude and transient decreases in turning amplitude (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by peak-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Triggering body posture amplitude to DVA activity peaks did not reveal any discernible signal.
source: Triggering body posture amplitude to DVA activity peaks did not reveal any discernible signal (Figure 8—figure supplement 1I); these findings highlight the strength of the eigenworm decomposition approach for decoding behavior from neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by peak-triggered average analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1I.

claim: DVA activity correlates to multiple aspects of behavior including the transition from forward to reverse movement and prolonged pausing.
source: In summary DVA activity correlates to multiple aspects of behavior including the transition from forward to reverse movement and prolonged pausing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the DVA calcium imaging data.

claim: Consistent with the role of DVA/NLP-12 in promoting undulation amplitude, DVA neural activity peaks co-occur with undulation amplitude increases and reciprocal turning amplitude decreases.
source: Consistent with the role of DVA/NLP-12 in promoting undulation amplitude (Figure 5C) DVA neural activity peaks co-occur with undulation amplitude increases and reciprocal turning amplitude decreases.
evidence: This is a conclusion connecting the neural activity data with the behavioral phenotype data.

claim: 1–1.5 hr food-deprived animals strongly avoided low O2 concentrations, accumulated at intermediate O2 concentrations around a bin center of 16.4% and slightly avoided atmospheric levels of 21% O2.
source: The average distribution profile suggested that 1–1.5 hr food-deprived animals strongly avoided low O2 concentrations, accumulated at intermediate O2 concentrations around a bin center of 16.4% and slightly avoided atmospheric levels of 21% O2 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: During control experiments with 21% O2 flow from both microdevice inlets, animals tended to slightly accumulate in the middle part of the arena.
source: For each experiment a paired control experiment was performed (21% O2 flow from both microdevice inlets), during which animals tended to slightly accumulate in the middle part of the arena (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In comparison to control experiments lacking a gradient, animals exhibited a curving bias towards preferred O2 concentrations, strongest at bearing orientations around 90°.
source: We then calculated the animals' curving bias, which is the average change in the bearing trajectory ΔB/Δx as a function of bearing (Figure 9C–D). In comparison to control experiments lacking a gradient, animals exhibited a curving bias towards preferred O2 concentrations, strongest at bearing orientations around 90° (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by curving bias analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Reversal rates were suppressed or increased at low or high bearing angles, respectively.
source: Next, we investigated the modulation of reorientation rate and found that reversal rates were suppressed or increased at low or high bearing angles, respectively (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by reversal rate analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: A gradual reduction of locomotion speed was observed as a function of increased bearing angles.
source: We also observed a gradual reduction of locomotion speed as a function of increased bearing angles (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by speed analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: On average, turning increased gradually as a function of bearing angles during O2 chemotaxis but not under control conditions.
source: Finally, we detected individual shallow turning events based on finding local peaks of turning mode signal of the mid-body during forward locomotion, excluding omega turns. On average, turning increased gradually as a function of bearing angles during O2 chemotaxis but not under control conditions (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by turning event analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Wild type N2 animals when fasted for 1–1.5 hr perform O2 chemotaxis to approach intermediate O2 concentrations centered around 16.4%.
source: In summary, we found that wild type N2 animals when fasted for 1–1.5 hr perform O2 chemotaxis to approach intermediate O2 concentrations centered around 16.4%.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the chemotaxis assay data presented in Figure 9.

claim: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed a defect in their ability to distribute in response to the O2 gradient.
source: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed a defect in their ability to distribute in response to the O2 gradient (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by spatial distribution data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed a compromised ability to avoid low O2 concentrations.
source: We subtracted the fractional animal distributions during controls from the distributions during gradient application in order to calculate O2 chemotaxis indices for low O2 concentration ranges. This revealed a compromised ability of flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants to avoid low O2 concentrations (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis index analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A similar defect in O2 chemotaxis was observed in nlp-12 and flp-1 single mutants but not in AVK- animals.
source: A similar defect was observed in nlp-12 and flp-1 single mutants but not in AVK- animals (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: flp-1 single mutants as well as AVK- animals showed a stronger tendency to accumulate in the center of the assay arena during control experiments.
source: However, flp-1 single mutants as well as AVK- animals showed a stronger tendency to accumulate in the center of the assay arena during control experiments (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: nlp-12 mutants as well as flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed reduced weathervaning O2 chemotaxis.
source: nlp-12 mutants as well as flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed reduced weathervaning O2 chemotaxis (Figure 10C; Figure 10—figure supplement 1E) but were able to modulate reversal rates (Figure 10D; Figure 10—figure supplement 1F) despite lower reversal rates in nlp-12 single mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by weathervaning analysis shown in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 1E.

claim: nlp-12 mutants and flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants were able to modulate reversal rates during O2 chemotaxis.
source: nlp-12 mutants as well as flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants showed reduced weathervaning O2 chemotaxis (Figure 10C; Figure 10—figure supplement 1E) but were able to modulate reversal rates (Figure 10D; Figure 10—figure supplement 1F) despite lower reversal rates in nlp-12 single mutants (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by reversal rate analysis shown in Figure 10D and Figure 10—figure supplement 1F.

claim: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants did not modulate locomotion speed and turning mode as a function of bearing.
source: flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants did not modulate locomotion speed and turning mode as a function of bearing (Figure 10E,F); both parameters were modulated in nlp-12 single mutants despite low and high basal rates in speed and body turning signal, respectively (Figure 10—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by speed and turning analysis shown in Figure 10E-F.

claim: When both FLP-1 and NLP-12 signaling is abolished, animals exhibit specific defects in navigating O2 gradients: both weathervaning at intermediate bearing angles and up-regulation of ARS-like behaviors at high bearing angles are compromised; however, modulation of reversal rates as a function of bearing angle is unaffected.
source: Taken together, these results show that when both FLP-1 and NLP-12 signaling is abolished, animals exhibit specific defects in navigating O2 gradients: both weathervaning at intermediate bearing angles and up-regulation of ARS-like behaviors, i.e. slowing and increased turning, at high bearing angles are compromised; however, modulation of reversal rates as a function of bearing angle is unaffected.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the chemotaxis analysis of flp-1;nlp-12 double mutants presented in Figure 10.

claim: The undulation mode describes regular forward and backward crawling, onto which the turning mode imposes turning movements.
source: This work shows how a nervous system controls simple elementary features of posture to generate complex movements for goal-directed locomotion strategies.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: The fine-tuned control of undulation and turning motions is essential for normal navigation of spatial gradients.
source: These data indicate that the fine-tuned control of undulation and turning motions is essential for normal navigation of spatial gradients; nevertheless, the biased random walk strategy can partially compensate for these deficits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chemotaxis defects observed in mutant animals.

claim: The biased random walk strategy can partially compensate for deficits in weathervaning and ARS-like behavior modulation during chemotaxis.
source: These data indicate that the fine-tuned control of undulation and turning motions is essential for normal navigation of spatial gradients; nevertheless, the biased random walk strategy can partially compensate for these deficits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mutant animals retain some chemotaxis ability despite defects in other strategies.

claim: In bacteria the biased random walk strategy is the only reported mechanism supporting the organism to reach its goal.
source: In bacteria the biased random walk strategy is the only reported mechanism supporting the organism to reach its goal (Berg and Brown, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on bacterial chemotaxis.

claim: Combination of elementary motor patterns enables animals to flexibly adjust their locomotion strategy.
source: In conclusion, we propose that combination of elementary motor patterns enables animals to flexibly adjust their locomotion strategy.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's main finding.

claim: The undulation mode dominates LDT while turning movements shape O2-induced ARS.
source: The undulation mode dominates LDT while turning movements shape O2-induced ARS.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the relative contributions of the two motor modes to different behavioral strategies.

claim: LDT and O2-induced ARS behaviors lie on a continuum.
source: However, these behaviors lie on a continuum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gradual nature of behavioral changes observed in response to oxygen stimuli.

claim: Neuromodulatory peptidergic circuits gradually adjust the underlying movement parameters while enforcing lawful reciprocal relationships between them.
source: Neuromodulatory peptidergic circuits gradually adjust the underlying movement parameters while enforcing lawful reciprocal relationships between them.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the role of the AVK/FLP-1 and DVA/NLP-12 systems in controlling locomotion.

claim: Movement can be finely controlled according to the animals' instantaneous needs, allowing for a rapid sensory-evoked shift from LDT to O2-induced ARS as well as for subtle movement changes during navigation.
source: In this way, movement can be finely controlled according to the animals' instantaneous needs, allowing for a rapid sensory-evoked shift from LDT to O2-induced ARS as well as for subtle movement changes during navigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the functional significance of the motor control system described in the study.

claim: The coordination of motor patterns for foraging accounts for a tradeoff that animals have to make in order to effectively achieve the goals of each strategy: fast undulation requires a coherent coordination of all body parts, while slow search movements require flexibility in gait and posture.
source: The coordination of motor patterns for foraging accounts for a tradeoff that animals have to make in order to effectively achieve the goals of each strategy: fast undulation requires a coherent coordination of all body parts, while slow search movements require flexibility in gait and posture.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the functional significance of the tradeoff between different locomotion strategies.

claim: Analogous control schemes may govern locomotion in higher animals.
source: In this work we provide experimental support for this concept obtained from C. elegans and speculate that analogous control schemes may govern locomotion in higher animals.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential generalizability of the findings to other animals.
